PLEXOS and GTMax SL models run up to this point in the modeling process used generic FES customer 
hourly loads that were scaled each month to match SLCA/IP hydropower production. The next two 
procedures optimize FES customer hourly loads (delivered SLCA/IP energy requests under FES contract 
terms) from a grid perspective. These loads are then input into a second round of GTMax SL runs. The 
first procedure computes the total obligation over all FES customer contracts based on GTMax SL from 
the first set of runs. It computes hydropower monthly maximum and minimum output levels and total 
monthly generation amounts for all SLCA/IP hydropower plants. 
Next, this total FES obligation is disaggregated into customer-level contracts that in PLEXOS represent 
dispatchable supply resources with minimum, maximum, and total energy constraints. The grid location 
of each modeled FES contract is based on the bus(es) where customer native loads reside. To avoid 
double-counting SLCA/IP hydropower energy injections into the grid are turned off. The PLEXOS model 
results are time series of geographically based FES customer requests for SLCA/IP hydropower. These 
customer-level requests are then totaled each hour and input into GTMax SL as fixed FES loads. FES 
customer load magnitudes and temporal shapes are specific to VRE and hydropower case and, in most 
situations, depart significantly from historical loads. 
Generation profiles for all small hydropower facilities input into this second round of GTMax SL are 
identical to the first set of runs. However, Molina hydropower plant block generation is block-loaded 
(either off or operated at capacity) based on monthly FES hourly load patterns. Because monthly FES 
customer load patterns differ by scenario, Molinia operations are scenario specific. 
4.5.4. SERM Network Given/FIXED SLCA/IP Energy Supplies 
SERM determines optimal pathways that “contractually” transport SLCA/IP energy from supply source 
nodes to energy sink nodes via transmission links. Supply resources include SLCA/IP hydropower 
resources that are represented in GTMax SL and power purchases at market hubs. Energy sinks include 
FES customer loads that are assigned to power grid PODs and energy sales at market trading points. 
Bidirectional line flow limits are set for each link. Limits are also placed on a group of links. Individual 
line and link group limits may vary hourly. Existing and/or anticipated sales of a transmission capacity on 
predefined pathway to a third-party entity are subtracted from specified link capacity limits and, if 
applicable, one or more groups of links. Modeled contractual transmission flows typically do not exceed 
line capacity limits but may exceed limits at a very high cost; that is, the limits are soft constraints. 
SERM also simulates SRP Exchange agreements with the CRSP Office in which generation from the SRP 
Craig, Hayden, and Four Corners thermal power plants serve CRSP FES customer loads in the northern 
48 
 
and Four Corners area of the SLCA/IP footprint. In exchange, on a one-for-one megawatt-hour basis 
during the same hour, GCD generation is delivered to the SRP POD. Under the SRP agreement, energy is 
also wheeled from SRP thermal power plants to the SRP POD. 
Because of transmission constraints and transmission energy losses in the grid, prices vary across the 
SLCA/IP footprint. CRSP energy marketers utilize its far-reaching transmission network to strategically 
buy and sell energy at various locations in its footprint. Therefore, market prices at purchase and sale 
node (e.g., market hubs) are typically different from the price at GCD (i.e., a measure of GCD economic 
energy value). SERM optimizes hourly energy market purchases and sales within transmission link limits. 
 
49 
 
5. Study Results 
This section presents study results focusing on the research questions posed in the introduction of this 
paper. Results include an examination of plausible WI capacity expansion pathways focusing on futures 
with a range of VRE build-outs and associated impacts on GCD hydropower operations under both 
normal and lowest-trace hydropower conditions. It also provides insights into both the impacts of 
evolving grid paradigms on the physical WI transmission system and on contractual power flows within 
the SLCA/IP system. Lastly, this section discusses future WI grid reliability and the capability of the GCD 
hydropower plant to provide ancillary services in the future. 
5.1. GCD Monthly Generation and FES Customer DSA Offers 
Figure 17 shows monthly SLCA/IP delivered hydropower energy (generation minus losses) and annual 
contributions from the GCD hydropower plant. Note that under the Current VRE case (2024), annual 
GCD generation for the lowest hydropower trace is only 225 gigawatt-hours (GWh) (8%) less than the 
normal hydropower trace. This drop in generation is due to a decrease in Lake Powell’s water elevation 
resulting in a lower water-to-power conversion rate. According to CRMMS, monthly 2024 water release 
volumes are identical for all traces, including both normal and lowest hydropower traces; that is, for this 
initial simulation year the CRMMS model does not adjust monthly water release volumes in response to 
Lake Powell inflow levels.

Under the Moderate VRE scenario (2036), CRMMS adjusts water reservoir water releases in response to

showed a relatively small reduction in generation under the lowest-trace hydropower condition, the 
Moderate VRE case (2036) GCD annual generation for the lowest-trace hydropower condition is zero. 
This occurs because the Lake Powell Reservoir water elevation is projected to be below the minimum 
power pool elevation during the entire year. SLCA/IP hydropower generation shown in Figure 17 is 
produced entirely by the other SLCA/IP hydropower plants. 
Under the High VRE case (2050) with the lowest-trace hydropower condition, the water elevation at 
Lake Powell is above the minimum power pool level for only 4 months of the year (July through 
October). The rest of the year GCD produces zero energy. 
Because it is assumed that DSA marketing rules apply, FES customer monthly energy offers are set equal 
to SLCA/IP hydropower generation minus transmission losses. FES customers must therefore adjust the 
use of energy supplies, including power purchases, accordingly. 
5.2. Impacts to Western Interconnection Generation 
The top of Figure 18 shows annual PLEXOS results for six scenarios: Current VRE, Moderate VRE, and 
High VRE cases each paired with normal and lowest-trace (labeled as worst-case) GCD hydropower 
generation. The figure shows that the normal and lowest-trace hydrology cases for the Current VRE case 
are similar. However, in the Moderate VRE case, the normal hydropower scenario looks similar to the 
Current VRE case, but the lowest-trace hydropower scenario produces 0 GWh on an annual basis, 
meaning that Lake Powell is below the minimum elevation for power production for the full year. 
Somewhat similarly, the High VRE case illustrates normal and lowest-trace hydropower scenarios that 
are substantially different. In the lowest-trace hydropower case, GCD does not generate any electricity 
for the majority of the months of the year but does generate for a few months in the late fall and 
winter. First, we note that although hydropower plays a large part in the total generation mix of the 
Western Interconnection, Glen Canyon forms a small part of the overall total, and the lowest-trace Glen 
Canyon generation doesn’t impact the total generation mix to a noticeable degree. 
The bottom of Figure 18 shows the difference between the two hydropower scenarios, where the drop 
in hydropower (negative y-axis) must be balanced by an increase in generation from other sources. The 
lowest trace is much more impactful in the Moderate and High VRE cases, and the loss of Glen Canyon 
hydropower generation is replaced by increased power produced from a mix of other resources on the 
system, particularly natural gas generation, but also in small part generation from coal, wind, and solar. 
The CRB area is a net exporter of electricity, meaning they have more generation than needed to serve 
their load due to the somewhat sparse population relative to other parts of the WI. Figure 19 quantifies 
the monthly exports out of the CRB region for the six annual PLEXOS simulations. Relative to the normal 
hydropower case, loss of GCD generation under other lower hydropower conditions does not have a 
significant impact on either the monthly energy export out of the region or power flows on an aggregate 
basis, although the impact is slightly more noticeable in the Moderate and High VRE cases. This indicates 
that there are sufficient local generation resources to cover much of the deficit when GCD generation is 
51 
 
lost, although there is some minimal loss of export ability from the CRB region to the surrounding 
regions. Again, this finding reiterates that although GCD is a large generation asset, it is one piece of a 
large fleet, so loss of generation at GCD can be compensated by other parts of the whole. We also note 
that export capability on the whole goes down slightly (less than 10%) for this region between the 
Current VRE, Moderate VRE, and High VRE cases, but not substantially. The slight reduction occurs due 
to shifts in load and generation resources but illustrates that the region expects to remain an exporter of 
electricity throughout all scenarios.

5.3. GCD Impact on WI Reliability 
Due to the relatively small impact of the loss of GCD generation compared to the size of the rest of the 
WI, there are no concerning reliability impacts to highlight in any of the six scenarios. In this case, we 
quantify reliability impacts by measuring unserved energy (dropped load), and there is zero unserved 
energy in the entire WI across all cases, indicating sufficient operating margin to meet the loss in 
generation associated with reduced hydrology. We can also examine hours with unserved reserves, 
which may occur during hours of scarcity when reserve providers may be called upon to provide actual 
energy to cope with system needs. There are a small number of hours of unserved reserves (around 10 
hours) in the 2036 case; however, the number of hours does not increase in the lowest-trace 
hydropower scenario, indicating that the reserve shortage is not due to loss of generation at GCD itself. 
The High VRE case has no hours of reserve shortage. We do note that there are occasional impacts on 
prices in very specific regions. For instance, Figure 20 shows the average locational marginal price for 
the month of August for the CRB region. It shows similar prices for the entire average day, but the peak 
price (occurring at 6 p.m.) is observably higher in the lowest-trace hydropower scenario relative to the 
normal hydropower case. Although there are other metrics for system reliability that require even more 
detailed modeling tools and analysis, this hourly unit commitment and economic dispatch modeling 
effort does not yield any concerns for wider system reliability. 
However, there are several caveats to note. First, we capture only hourly balancing, not sub-hourly. We 
also employ a reduced transmission network by aggregating outside transmission lines outside of the 
CRB focus region. We also do not capture the impacts to the distribution system or transmission outages 
caused for planned or unplanned reasons. We also do not consider the forecast error incurred by load, 
wind, or solar. Lastly, we do not consider hydrology (drought) impacts to other river systems in the WI, 
only the impacts to Lake Powell and thus Glen Canyon generation station. In reality, impacts to other 
dams along the Colorado River and elsewhere in the West could have reliability impacts beyond the 
local effects studied here and should be considered in future work. 
54 
 
 
5.4. Energy Market Transactions 
FES customers that receive SLCA/IP hydropower generation under contractual agreements with WAPA 
are bound by maximum (capacity) and minimum schedule requirement restrictions. Also, under DSA 
rules, the amount of monthly energy that customers receive is set equal to projected SLCA/IP 
hydropower generation minus delivery losses that are incurred via the transport of energy from 
hydropower plants to FES customer points of delivery. 
Contract terms for FES monthly capacity and energy offers are determined by the CRSP Office quarterly. 
Assuming perfect water and hydropower forecasts, no transmission restrictions, and unlimited 
hydropower operational flexibility, there would be no energy market transactions because CRSP 
operating guidelines specify that hourly SLCA/IP hydropower deliveries should serve FES customer loads. 
However, energy market transactions occur because: 
(1) There are many restrictions that bind the operation of SLCA/IP hydropower resources such as 
hourly water ramp limits, while FES contracts have significantly fewer restrictions; that is, 
contracts terms are more flexible than hydropower operations. 
(2) The delivery of SLCA/IP hydropower productions to FES customer points of delivery is subject to 
contractual transmission line limits. 
Quantified by the GTMax SL model, Cause 1 above requires energy purchases during hours in a month 
when SLCA/IP hydropower generation cannot ramp up fast enough or reach levels high enough to serve 
all DSA loads (short position). On the other hand, energy sales are required during hours when 
hydropower generation cannot ramp down fast enough or reduce output low enough to follow load 
(long position). Because DSA requires that total energy offers during a month equals total SLCA/IP 
 
Figure 20. Prices weighted by generation in the Colorado River Basin region for highest load days of the 
simulated year under the Current VRE, August 24 (2024). 
 

55 
 
hydropower energy deliveries, total purchases during energy short hours must exactly equal total 
energy sales during long energy hours to maintain a system energy balance. Furthermore, because the 
CRSP Offices strives to minimize energy transactions, the copperplate methodology does not allow both 
purchases and sales during the same hour. 
On the other hand, transmission constraints (Cause 2) force purchases and sales of identical amounts in 
the same hour but at different locations. These energy transactions are both identified by and quantified 
by SERM. 
In some cases, all energy market transactions are due to Cause 1 while some transactions are solely 
caused by transmission limitation. Under other circumstances, both Cause 1 and Cause 2 apply.

5.3. GCD Impact on WI Reliability 
Due to the relatively small impact of the loss of GCD generation compared to the size of the rest of the 
WI, there are no concerning reliability impacts to highlight in any of the six scenarios. In this case, we 
quantify reliability impacts by measuring unserved energy (dropped load), and there is zero unserved 
energy in the entire WI across all cases, indicating sufficient operating margin to meet the loss in 
generation associated with reduced hydrology. We can also examine hours with unserved reserves, 
which may occur during hours of scarcity when reserve providers may be called upon to provide actual 
energy to cope with system needs. There are a small number of hours of unserved reserves (around 10 
hours) in the 2036 case; however, the number of hours does not increase in the lowest-trace 
hydropower scenario, indicating that the reserve shortage is not due to loss of generation at GCD itself. 
The High VRE case has no hours of reserve shortage. We do note that there are occasional impacts on 
prices in very specific regions. For instance, Figure 20 shows the average locational marginal price for 
the month of August for the CRB region. It shows similar prices for the entire average day, but the peak 
price (occurring at 6 p.m.) is observably higher in the lowest-trace hydropower scenario relative to the 
normal hydropower case. Although there are other metrics for system reliability that require even more 
detailed modeling tools and analysis, this hourly unit commitment and economic dispatch modeling 
effort does not yield any concerns for wider system reliability. 
However, there are several caveats to note. First, we capture only hourly balancing, not sub-hourly. We 
also employ a reduced transmission network by aggregating outside transmission lines outside of the 
CRB focus region. We also do not capture the impacts to the distribution system or transmission outages 
caused for planned or unplanned reasons. We also do not consider the forecast error incurred by load, 
wind, or solar. Lastly, we do not consider hydrology (drought) impacts to other river systems in the WI, 
only the impacts to Lake Powell and thus Glen Canyon generation station. In reality, impacts to other 
dams along the Colorado River and elsewhere in the West could have reliability impacts beyond the 
local effects studied here and should be considered in future work.

5.4. Energy Market Transactions 
FES customers that receive SLCA/IP hydropower generation under contractual agreements with WAPA 
are bound by maximum (capacity) and minimum schedule requirement restrictions. Also, under DSA 
rules, the amount of monthly energy that customers receive is set equal to projected SLCA/IP 
hydropower generation minus delivery losses that are incurred via the transport of energy from 
hydropower plants to FES customer points of delivery. 
Contract terms for FES monthly capacity and energy offers are determined by the CRSP Office quarterly. 
Assuming perfect water and hydropower forecasts, no transmission restrictions, and unlimited 
hydropower operational flexibility, there would be no energy market transactions because CRSP 
operating guidelines specify that hourly SLCA/IP hydropower deliveries should serve FES customer loads.

hourly water ramp limits, while FES contracts have significantly fewer restrictions; that is, 
contracts terms are more flexible than hydropower operations.

contractual transmission line limits.

by SERM.

64 
 
6. Conclusions 
This study was conducted under the 2020 Federal Hydropower Memorandum of Understanding 
between WAPA, DOE, and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. It analyzes how the evolving WI grid may 
potentially change the future operation of the GCD hydropower plant under normal and lowest 
projected hydropower conditions in terms of hydropower plant capacity and annual energy production. 
To conclude, we reiterate our research questions and summarize the findings in each category. 
What are some plausible WI grid futures? 
To assess the impact of GCD hydropower plant changes on the wider WI, we started with a 
representation of possible future evolution based on the NARIS study, which used advanced 
optimization modeling to determine how power system investments may occur. In this representation 
of the WI, we observe continued growth of wind and solar capacity, and continuing importance of 
natural gas and hydropower generation. We use three scenarios, a Current VRE case (approximately 
reflecting the generation mix of 2024), a Moderate VRE case (representing a future 2036 mix), and a 
High VRE case (representing a future 2050 mix). 
How will GCD hydropower resources evolve? 
This study considered many hydrological traces for GCD hydropower resources into the future from 
which we selected “normal” trace and “lowest” trace hydropower conditions for each of the three grid 
mixes described above. These traces show that under normal GCD hydropower conditions annual 
capacity and energy levels are similar to current levels. However, GCD hourly generation patterns are 
expected to evolve as FES customers change the scheduling of WAPA energy under contract because 
VRE expansion affects two primary scheduling drivers namely, market prices and net system load 
profiles. Because FES contract terms are more flexible than SLCA/IP hydropower operating criteria, at 
times, schedules submitted by customers change more rapidly than SLCA/IP hydropower response 
times. This results in a hydropower operation schedule that deviates from FES customer loads whereby 
energy purchases are required in some hours and sales are required during other hours. 
Under the lowest-trace condition, GCD hydropower shows a modest drop in energy production from 
GCD under the Current VRE case (2024) due to a drop in Lake Powell Reservoir water elevation. 
However, under the Moderate VRE case (2036), annual GCD generation is zero because the water 
elevation in Lake Powell drops below the minimum power pool level during the entire year. Under the 
High VRE case (2050) GCD generation is also zero during most of the year. However, it produces 
relatively small amounts of energy during a 4-month period from the beginning of July through the end 
of October. Production levels are significantly less than normal during these 4 months because the 
hydraulic head is relatively low, resulting in a low water-to-power conversion. Also, monthly water 
release volumes are significantly less than normal. 
 
65 
 
How much capacity and energy will the WAPA CRSP Office offer its FES customers in the future? 
It is assumed that the CRSP Office will continue to use the DSA methodology as the basis for making FES 
capacity and energy offers to its customers in the future. Therefore, there is a direct relationship 
between hydropower conditions and FES customer offers. Consistent with the response to the previous 
research question, offers for the normal hydropower condition are expected to be similar to current 
levels under all three VRE capacity expansion cases. However, when GCD generation levels fall to zero, 
DSA offers are based solely on hydropower capacity and energy produced by the other SLCA/IP 
hydropower plants. Under the Moderate VRE case (2036) annual energy offers are less than 20% of 
current levels during the lowest-trace hydropower condition; that is offers drop by about 80%. Offers 
under lowest-trace hydropower conditions for the High VRE case drop by more than 60%. 
Will future GCD hydropower operations significantly impact physical and contractual power flows? 
We find that future changes to GCD hydropower operations may impact physical power flows 
occasionally and transiently; however, the overall power flow did not change much with GCD generation 
in most cases. We do note a reduced export capability in the region from the total loss of GCD 
generation, but alternative sources are largely available in the region to make up the loss. These 
alternative sources are mostly natural gas fired generation with small contributions from increased coal, 
wind, and solar generation. 
On the other hand, SLCA/IP transmission system contractual power flows are expected to change 
dramatically. These findings assume that the SRP exchange will not continue in the future. In general, 
when it operates, GCD generation creates a regional energy surplus in the southern region. Similar to 
current operations, the excess energy is transported to the Four Corners and northern regions to resolve 
energy short positions in those areas. However, when GCD does not operate because Lake Powell’s 
water is below the minimum power pool, there is an energy shortfall in the southern region that is 
resolved by SLCA/IP hydropower generation in the northern region where there is an energy oversupply. 
In other words, contractual power flows are reversed relative to current flows when GCD does not 
produce power. 
What CRSP transmission lines will be most often contractually binding in the future? 
When FES point of delivery loads are low, contractual power flow among the regions also tends to be 
relatively low and transmission line limits are not binding. In all situations when GCD does not operate 
and FES loads are light in alignment with DSA practices, the modeling results show that there are no 
binding contractual power flows on any transmission line. 
However, when monthly hydropower conditions are normal and loads are high, such as during some on-
peak hours, all the southern surplus energy cannot be transported from the GCD hydropower plant to 
the Shiprock substation because of binding contractual line limits. Therefore, some of the surplus energy 
must be sold at a market hub located in the southern region. This creates a shortfall in the northern and 
Four Corners regions during the same hour where energy purchases at the lowest-cost market hub 
resolve these regional energy imbalances. 
66 
 
Will WI grid reliability be impacted by operational changes at GCD (hydropower capacity and grid 
power flow)? 
We found that WI grid reliability was not largely impacted by operational changes at GCD. The WI grid is 
a large and interconnected system, and although GCD is a large and substantial generation resource, it is 
a small piece of a much larger system. We found that other generation resources were able to make up 
the deficit resulting from loss of generation at GCD, resulting in no unserved energy or dropped load 
across scenarios. 
Will the GCD hydropower plant be capable of serving ancillary services in the future? 
Modeling results show that GCD will be able to provide spinning and regulation services in all situations 
except when it does not operate, that is, when the Lake Powell Reservoir water elevation is below the 
minimum power pool level. 
 
 
 
 
 
67

ATTACHMENT A: Western Area Power Administration and Federal 
Hydropower Project Overview 
The Western Area Power Administration (WAPA) is a federal power marketing administration under U.S. 
Department of Energy (DOE). Figure A 1 shows a map of WAPA marketing areas that are managed by 
various regional offices. Each region is unique in terms of their hydropower and transmission resources, 
statutory requirements, operating criteria/goals, contractual arrangements with their firm electric 
service (FES) customers and obligations to serve project use loads.2 
 
Figure A 1. Map of WAPA marketing areas and regional offices 
The WAPA Colorado River Storage Project (CRSP) Office markets, sells, and delivers upper Colorado River 
Basin (CRB) energy to public and municipal entities in Utah, Wyoming, Nebraska, Colorado, New Mexico, 
Arizona, and Nevada (Bureau of Reclamation 2022). It also provides for the comprehensive development 
of upper CRB hydropower, 2,300 miles of transmission lines, and 35 high-voltage transformers. Upper 
CRB hydropower plants generate an annual average of 5.75 terawatt-hours energy. Major CRSP 
hydropower resources include Upper and Lower Molina, Fontenelle, Flaming Gorge, Blue Mesa, Morrow 
Point, Crystal, and Glen Canyon. 
 
 
 
2 Other marketing areas within WAPA include the Loveland Area Projects, Central Valley and Washoe projects, 
Falcon-Amistad Project, Provo River Project, Pick-Sloan Missouri Basin Program, and the Salt Lake City Area 
Projects. 

70 
 
ATTACHMENT B: Colorado River Basin 
The Colorado River Basin (CRB) is about 1,450 miles long, with headwaters in Colorado and Wyoming. 
The basin drainage area of about 246,000 square miles includes all of Arizona and parts of California, 
Colorado, New Mexico, Nevada, Utah, and Wyoming. It is managed and operated under numerous 
compacts, federal laws, court decisions and decrees, contracts, and regulatory guidelines collectively 
known as the "Law of the River" (Bureau of Reclamation 2015). Within these legal mandates, the Bureau 
of Reclamation (Reclamation) plays a major role in the control and distribution of surface water through 
the management of water storage and releases from CRB federal reservoirs (U.S. Geological Survey 
2018). Within Reclamation water release directives, the Western Area Power Administration (WAPA) 
schedules CRB hydropower plant-level hourly energy production from approximately 4,200 megawatts 
of installed capacity, and Reclamation dispatches and operates individual generating units in real time. 
WAPA is part of the U.S. Department of Energy, and Reclamation is a federal agency under 
the U.S. Department of the Interior.3 
The Colorado River Compact of 1922 divided the CRB into upper and lower drainage areas and allocated 
the river’s water resources into two groups of states aligned with these areas. As shown on the map in 
Figure 1 in the main text, the dividing point on the Colorado River between the upper and lower CRB is 
near the northern border of Arizona at Lees Ferry, 15 river miles downstream of the Glen Canyon Dam. 
Water management between the upper and lower CRB is guided by the Record of Decision for 
“Colorado River Interim Guidelines for Lower Basin Shortages and Coordinated Operations for Lake 
Powell and Lake Mead.” It outlines the strategy for coordinating the operations of Lake Powell (upper-
basin reservoir with the lowest upper-basin elevation) and downstream Lake Mead (lower-basin 
reservoir with the highest lower-basin elevation). The objectives of these coordinated operations are “to 
avoid curtailment of uses in the Upper Basin, minimize shortages in the Lower Basin and not adversely 
affect the yield for development available in the Upper Basin” (Bureau of Reclamation 2020). 
 
 
3 WAPA and Reclamation are cooperating federal agencies. 
71 
 
ATTACHMENT C: Historical VRE Capacity Build-Out and Energy 
Production in the Western Interconnection 
The generation capacity in the Western Interconnection has undergone shifts, as shown in Figure A 2 
(Western Electricity Coordinating Council 2025a). Cost advancements for solar, wind, and battery 
technologies have increased their competitiveness and resulted in their growth on the electricity grid. 
In the near term, the Western Interconnection expects these trends to continue and has noted that they 
expect 80% of capacity additions in 2025 to be solar, battery, and wind. Similar to the trend in the West 
as a whole, renewable resources have increased in the two Western Area Power Administration 
balancing authorities. 
 
 
 
Figure C-1. Historical 2015–2024 capacity additions by type of energy resource 
Figure A 2. Historical 2015-2024 capacity by type of energy resource 
72 
 
ATTACHMENT D: Western Interconnection Power Grid 
The Western Interconnection (WI) power grid, one of the three main synchronous grids that powers 
North America, serves a population of over 80 million people. A single entity, the Western Electricity 
Coordinating Council, is responsible for monitoring WI reliability, compliance enforcement, and violation 
mitigation. The interconnection spans 1.8 million square miles, encompassing 10 states and parts of four 
other states, the Canadian provinces of British Columbia and Alberta, and the northern part of Baja 
California in Mexico. Due to the unique geography, demography, and history, the WI is distinct in many 
ways from the other North America interconnections (Western Electricity Coordinating Council 2025b). 
Historically, there has been less reliance on market structures. Since 2011, there has been a gradual 
expansion of market participation by balancing authorities, with a majority of western balancing 
authorities participating in either the CAISO Energy Imbalance Market or the Southwest Power Pool 
Western Energy Imbalance Service market. 
Within its geographical footprint, the WI is projected to increase wind and solar power production, 
retire several coal-fired power plants, and increase its reliance on highly efficient and flexible natural-
gas-fired technologies. In total, these measures are expected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and 
change locational marginal price levels and patterns.

ATTACHMENT A: Western Area Power Administration and Federal 
Hydropower Project Overview 
The Western Area Power Administration (WAPA) is a federal power marketing administration under U.S. 
Department of Energy (DOE). Figure A 1 shows a map of WAPA marketing areas that are managed by 
various regional offices. Each region is unique in terms of their hydropower and transmission resources, 
statutory requirements, operating criteria/goals, contractual arrangements with their firm electric 
service (FES) customers and obligations to serve project use loads.2 
 
Figure A 1. Map of WAPA marketing areas and regional offices 
The WAPA Colorado River Storage Project (CRSP) Office markets, sells, and delivers upper Colorado River 
Basin (CRB) energy to public and municipal entities in Utah, Wyoming, Nebraska, Colorado, New Mexico, 
Arizona, and Nevada (Bureau of Reclamation 2022). It also provides for the comprehensive development 
of upper CRB hydropower, 2,300 miles of transmission lines, and 35 high-voltage transformers. Upper 
CRB hydropower plants generate an annual average of 5.75 terawatt-hours energy. Major CRSP 
hydropower resources include Upper and Lower Molina, Fontenelle, Flaming Gorge, Blue Mesa, Morrow 
Point, Crystal, and Glen Canyon. 
 
 
 
2 Other marketing areas within WAPA include the Loveland Area Projects, Central Valley and Washoe projects, 
Falcon-Amistad Project, Provo River Project, Pick-Sloan Missouri Basin Program, and the Salt Lake City Area 
Projects. 

70 
 
ATTACHMENT B: Colorado River Basin 
The Colorado River Basin (CRB) is about 1,450 miles long, with headwaters in Colorado and Wyoming. 
The basin drainage area of about 246,000 square miles includes all of Arizona and parts of California, 
Colorado, New Mexico, Nevada, Utah, and Wyoming. It is managed and operated under numerous 
compacts, federal laws, court decisions and decrees, contracts, and regulatory guidelines collectively 
known as the "Law of the River" (Bureau of Reclamation 2015). Within these legal mandates, the Bureau 
of Reclamation (Reclamation) plays a major role in the control and distribution of surface water through 
the management of water storage and releases from CRB federal reservoirs (U.S. Geological Survey 
2018). Within Reclamation water release directives, the Western Area Power Administration (WAPA) 
schedules CRB hydropower plant-level hourly energy production from approximately 4,200 megawatts 
of installed capacity, and Reclamation dispatches and operates individual generating units in real time. 
WAPA is part of the U.S. Department of Energy, and Reclamation is a federal agency under 
the U.S. Department of the Interior.3 
The Colorado River Compact of 1922 divided the CRB into upper and lower drainage areas and allocated 
the river’s water resources into two groups of states aligned with these areas. As shown on the map in 
Figure 1 in the main text, the dividing point on the Colorado River between the upper and lower CRB is 
near the northern border of Arizona at Lees Ferry, 15 river miles downstream of the Glen Canyon Dam. 
Water management between the upper and lower CRB is guided by the Record of Decision for 
“Colorado River Interim Guidelines for Lower Basin Shortages and Coordinated Operations for Lake 
Powell and Lake Mead.” It outlines the strategy for coordinating the operations of Lake Powell (upper-
basin reservoir with the lowest upper-basin elevation) and downstream Lake Mead (lower-basin 
reservoir with the highest lower-basin elevation). The objectives of these coordinated operations are “to 
avoid curtailment of uses in the Upper Basin, minimize shortages in the Lower Basin and not adversely 
affect the yield for development available in the Upper Basin” (Bureau of Reclamation 2020). 
 
 
3 WAPA and Reclamation are cooperating federal agencies.

ATTACHMENT C: Historical VRE Capacity Build-Out and Energy 
Production in the Western Interconnection 
The generation capacity in the Western Interconnection has undergone shifts, as shown in Figure A 2 
(Western Electricity Coordinating Council 2025a). Cost advancements for solar, wind, and battery 
technologies have increased their competitiveness and resulted in their growth on the electricity grid. 
In the near term, the Western Interconnection expects these trends to continue and has noted that they 
expect 80% of capacity additions in 2025 to be solar, battery, and wind. Similar to the trend in the West 
as a whole, renewable resources have increased in the two Western Area Power Administration 
balancing authorities. 
 
 
 
Figure C-1. Historical 2015–2024 capacity additions by type of energy resource 
Figure A 2. Historical 2015-2024 capacity by type of energy resource

ATTACHMENT D: Western Interconnection Power Grid 
The Western Interconnection (WI) power grid, one of the three main synchronous grids that powers 
North America, serves a population of over 80 million people. A single entity, the Western Electricity 
Coordinating Council, is responsible for monitoring WI reliability, compliance enforcement, and violation 
mitigation. The interconnection spans 1.8 million square miles, encompassing 10 states and parts of four 
other states, the Canadian provinces of British Columbia and Alberta, and the northern part of Baja 
California in Mexico. Due to the unique geography, demography, and history, the WI is distinct in many 
ways from the other North America interconnections (Western Electricity Coordinating Council 2025b). 
Historically, there has been less reliance on market structures. Since 2011, there has been a gradual 
expansion of market participation by balancing authorities, with a majority of western balancing 
authorities participating in either the CAISO Energy Imbalance Market or the Southwest Power Pool 
Western Energy Imbalance Service market. 
Within its geographical footprint, the WI is projected to increase wind and solar power production, 
retire several coal-fired power plants, and increase its reliance on highly efficient and flexible natural-
gas-fired technologies. In total, these measures are expected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and 
change locational marginal price levels and patterns.

ATTACHMENT G: Physical, Institutional, and Environmental 
Constraints That Restrict Glen Canyon Dam 
The Glen Canyon Dam (GCD) located near Page, Arizona, is a key feature of the Colorado River Storage 
Project (CRSP). As shown in Figure A 5, the GCD is approximately 15 river-miles above Lees Ferry. This 
marks the beginning of 277 miles of Colorado River flows through the Grand Canyon and then on to Lake 
Mead, the reservoir for Hoover Dam. 
The 710-foot-high GCD structure forms Lake Powell behind it. When full, the lake stores 24 million acre-
feet of water. This corresponds to several years of water resources for GCD energy production and more 
storage capacity than all other CRSP resources combined. In addition to its water storage value, the 
power plant at GCD is a valuable component of the Western Interconnection power grid. 
The power plant at the toe of the dam is the largest hydroelectric facility in the CRSP system. It consists 
of eight 165-megawatt (MW) generators, each of which is driven by a Francis turbine, for a total 
nameplate generating capacity of 1,320 MW. The GCD hydropower plant accounts for about 75% of 
CRSP capacity and energy resources. It also supplies the grid with spinning reserve and both regulation-
up and regulation-down services. 
 
Figure A 5. Map of Glen Canyon, Lake Powell, and the Colorado River below the Glen Canyon Dam 
CRSP, and therefore the GCD hydropower plant, is integrated with the operation of other federal 
hydropower resources that are marketed by the Western Area Power Administration (WAPA). These 
resources include hydropower plants in the Seedskadee, Dolores, Collbran, and Rio Grande projects. 

76 
 
Hydropower generation schedules from all projects are managed by the CRSP Management Center. 
Located in Montrose, Colorado, the CRSP Management Center schedules federal hydropower resources 
to serve electricity demand for 5.8 million consumers in 10 western states that all reside in the Western 
Interconnection power grid. Plant-level production is scheduled by the CRSP Management Center on 
day-ahead, hour-ahead, and real time bases. Energy short and long positions are balanced by the CRSP 
Management Center via bilateral market transactions that span various lengths of time, typically ranging 
from seasonal to real time. 
Controlled water releases from Lake Powell via dam penstocks/outlets for energy production and non-
power routes (bypass tubes and spillways) have resulted in an altered aquatic and terrestrial ecosystem 
compared to the one that existed before the dam was built. Cold, clear water flows support a rainbow 
trout fishery in the river reach near the dam, while native fishes, including the endangered humpback 
chub (Gila cypha) and razorback sucker (Xyrauchen texanus), live farther downstream where water 
temperatures are warmer. Vegetation is established closer to the river’s edge than in the past due to the 
elimination of annual flood scouring and has increasingly become dominated by non-native plant 
species. 
Lake Powell, Lake Mead, and the Colorado River connecting these two reservoirs support important 
recreational resources. The regional recreation resources and the hydropower produced by GCD have 
important effects on local and regional economies. Additionally, the region’s natural resources are of 
vital importance to the social and economic well-being of Tribes with ancestral ties to Glen Canyon and 
Grand Canyon. Most cultural resources are located at higher elevations away from the area affected by 
dam operations, but operations at some locations may affect the availability of windblown sand that 
helps replenish eroded sites. 
Before 1990, GCD had few operating restrictions. Apart from a minimum water release requirement, its 
daily and hourly operations were constrained only by the physical limitations of the dam structure, the 
power plant, and the amount of water stored in and released from Lake Powell. Market price signals and 
temporal load profiles from CRSP firm electric service customers were the principal scheduling/dispatch 
drivers, often resulting in large hourly and daily fluctuations of the plant’s power output and associated 
water releases. 
Concerns about the impact of GCD operations on downstream ecosystems and endangered species, 
including those in Grand Canyon National Park, prompted Reclamation to conduct a series of 
experimental releases from June 1990 to July 1991 as part of an environmental studies program. Based 
on an analysis of these releases, Reclamation imposed operational flow constraints on Aug. 1, 1991. 
These constraints were in effect until February 1997, when new operational rules and management 
goals specified in the 1997 GCD Record of Decision were adopted. 
Rules and management goals were changed once more based on findings from a Long-Term 
Environmental Monitoring Plan Environmental Impact Study. The analysis identified environmental and 
economic issues and consequences associated with taking no action as well as a reasonable range of 
alternatives to no action. The alternatives addressed in the Long-Term Environmental Monitoring Plan 
77 
 
Environmental Impact Study included several operations and experimental actions that evaluated 
possible impacts from a range of criteria/actions, including the one that was selected under the 2016 
Record of Decision. 
The 2016 ROD specifies GCD operating rules, non-flow actions, and appropriate experimental and 
management actions that comply with the Grand Canyon Protection Act of 1992 requirements to 
minimize impacts on resources within the area impacted by dam operations. The water-operating 
criteria are specified by the 2016 Record of Decision for two time horizons: (1) monthly release volume 
targets and (2) restrictions that limit hourly operations within a day. These intra-day criteria limit hourly 
releases, changes in releases between two consecutive hours, and the range of hourly flows that occur 
during 24-hour rolling periods. Although not specifically mandated by the 2016 Record of Decision, 
WAPA and other interested parties have a non-binding agreement that restricts daily water release 
volumes. These restrictions are referred to as intra-monthly daily restrictions. 
The 2016 Record of Decision requires that Reclamation and WAPA periodically conduct various GCD 
experiments. These include High Flow Experiments and other types of experiments such as trout 
management flows and “bug” flows. As required, exceptions to intra-day operating criteria are also 
made to accommodate experimental releases. 
Table A-1 1 contains information from the 2016 Long-Term Environmental Monitoring Plan 
Environmental Impact Study final report. It provides an example of monthly release volume targets as a 
function of total annual water release. In general, Reclamation currently uses the values in this table to 
guide monthly release decisions.

In actual operations, the annual water target dictated by Reclamation mainly depends on the amount of 
water that is stored in Lake Powell, temporal inflows, and water delivery obligations. Monthly water 
releases, however, sometimes deviate from the plan to support a Long-Term Environmental Monitoring 
Plan experiment. For example, more water is shifted into a month when a High Flow Experiment is 
conducted. To comply with the annual release level, less water is therefore released during one or more 
months that do not have High Flow Experiments. 
In addition, water releases sometimes deviate from the levels shown in Table A-1 1 because of inflow 
forecast errors. Biannual and monthly water release volumes are planned by Reclamation prior to the 
beginning of each water year based on a forecast of future events. Actual events sometime deviate from 
these expectations, and plans for the next 24 months are revised as needed each month because of 
differences between actual events and previous projections.

least 5,000 cfs during the night. The criteria also limit how quickly the release rate can increase and

Located 155 miles below the Hoover Dam on the Colorado River, the Parker Dam authorized by the 
Rivers and Harbors Act of 1935 spans the Colorado River between Arizona and California. The Parker 
Dam is an arch structure built with 380,000 cubic yards of concrete. The crest of the dam is 856 feet long 
with a structural height of 320 feet; however, only 85 feet of the dam is above the riverbed. Water 
control is provided by five 50-ft-square gates.

ATTACHMENT H: Mapping of Individual CRSP to Loads at Specific 
PLEXOS Buses 
In order to map the WAPA customers to specific PLEXOS nodes, we used the name of the customer and

during 24-hour rolling periods. Although not specifically mandated by the 2016 Record of Decision, 
WAPA and other interested parties have a non-binding agreement that restricts daily water release 
volumes. These restrictions are referred to as intra-monthly daily restrictions. 
The 2016 Record of Decision requires that Reclamation and WAPA periodically conduct various GCD 
experiments. These include High Flow Experiments and other types of experiments such as trout 
management flows and “bug” flows. As required, exceptions to intra-day operating criteria are also 
made to accommodate experimental releases. 
Table A-1 1 contains information from the 2016 Long-Term Environmental Monitoring Plan 
Environmental Impact Study final report. It provides an example of monthly release volume targets as a 
function of total annual water release. In general, Reclamation currently uses the values in this table to 
guide monthly release decisions. 
In actual operations, the annual water target dictated by Reclamation mainly depends on the amount of 
water that is stored in Lake Powell, temporal inflows, and water delivery obligations. Monthly water 
releases, however, sometimes deviate from the plan to support a Long-Term Environmental Monitoring 
Plan experiment. For example, more water is shifted into a month when a High Flow Experiment is 
conducted. To comply with the annual release level, less water is therefore released during one or more 
months that do not have High Flow Experiments. 
In addition, water releases sometimes deviate from the levels shown in Table A-1 1 because of inflow 
forecast errors. Biannual and monthly water release volumes are planned by Reclamation prior to the 
beginning of each water year based on a forecast of future events. Actual events sometime deviate from 
these expectations, and plans for the next 24 months are revised as needed each month because of 
differences between actual events and previous projections. 
 
78

Some of the alternative operating criteria that were examined in support of the Long-Term 
Environmental Monitoring Plan Environmental Impact Study had monthly water release targets that 
differed from those shown above. Some were relatively less conducive for power economics relative to 
the 2016 Record of Decision while others yield higher economic values. 
The 2016 Record of Decision hourly restrictions are shown in Table A-1 2. It requires water release rates 
to be 8,000 cubic feet per second (cfs) or greater between the hours of 7:00 a.m. and 7:00 p.m., and at 
least 5,000 cfs during the night. The criteria also limit how quickly the release rate can increase and 
decrease between consecutive hours. The maximum hourly increase (i.e., the up-ramp rate) is 
4,000 cfs/hour, and the maximum hourly decrease (i.e., the down-ramp rate) is 2,500 cfs/hour. The 
2016 ROD operating criteria also restrict how much the releases can fluctuate during rolling 24-hour 
periods. This daily change (fluctuation) constraint varies monthly depending on the monthly volume of 
water release. Capped at 8,000 cfs, the daily fluctuation (in cfs) is equal to 10 times the monthly volume 
(in thousand acre-feet) from June to August and 9 times the monthly volume (in thousand acre-feet) 
during other months of the year. 
79

monthly volume (in thousand acre-feet) in other months; daily range not to exceed 8,000 cfs. 
The maximum release rate is limited to 25,000 cfs under the 2016 ROD operating criteria. Maximum 
flow rate exceptions are allowed to avoid spills and/or conduct flood releases during high runoff 
periods. Under these very wet hydrological conditions, when the average monthly release rate is greater 
than 25,000 cfs, water must be released at a constant rate during the entire month. 
Non-binding agreements restrict WAPA daily water release volumes during each month of the year. 
These restrictions are referred to as intra-monthly daily restrictions and do not change during the course 
of the year. The guidelines that WAPA has agreed to are as follows: 
(1) Weekday volumes are approximately the same each weekday throughout the month. 
(2) Saturday, Sunday, and holiday daily release volumes are no less than 85% of the weekday 
average. 
(3) Saturday, Sunday, and holiday daily release volumes are capped at the weekday average. 
Located 155 miles below the Hoover Dam on the Colorado River, the Parker Dam authorized by the 
Rivers and Harbors Act of 1935 spans the Colorado River between Arizona and California. The Parker 
Dam is an arch structure built with 380,000 cubic yards of concrete. The crest of the dam is 856 feet long 
with a structural height of 320 feet; however, only 85 feet of the dam is above the riverbed. Water 
control is provided by five 50-ft-square gates.

Executive Summary
Fish stranding has been studied in select rivers worldwide, often with the purpose of determining 
how to mitigate adverse effects of dam operations on highly valued salmon and trout populations. 
However, where a reduction in trout population size is desired by resource managers, as is the 
case downstream of the Glen Canyon Dam on the Colorado River, flow manipulations termed trout 
management flows (TMFs) may be used to optimize fish stranding and mortality. To inform the 
design and implementation of potential future TMFs, we reviewed relevant literature to identify 
key factors that influence fish stranding. We found that key factors were highly interdependent 
and site-specific, but general trends suggest that down-ramping (decreasing flow) at rapid rates 
in daytime during the late spring to summer emergence period would lead to stranding of age-0 
rainbow trout in shallow shoreline habitat. A hypsometric analysis was then used to predict 
stranding risk for age-0 rainbow trout in Glen Canyon for a range of TMFs, which incorporated 
existing bathymetric data and flow and habitat suitability models. Our results indicate that a 
TMF with a steady high flow ranging from 12,000 to 16,000 cubic feet per second (ft3/s) combined 
with a minimum flow ranging from 3,000 to 5,000 ft3/s may effectively strand age-0 fish while also 
minimizing risk to water storage in Lake Powell and other resources. This strategy implemented 
under normal hydropeaking operations was predicted to lead to a substantive stranding risk when 
paired with low flows of 5,000 ft3/s, and especially 3,000 ft3/s. However, there remains uncertainty 
associated with elements of implementing an effective TMF downstream from Glen Canyon Dam. 
The main uncertainties include (1) the down-ramp rate that maximizes stranding of age-0 trout, (2) 
the duration of drawdown to maximize stranding mortality while minimizing impact to downstream 
resources, (3) duration of high flows required for age-0 fish to colonize newly created shoreline 
habitat (this is only for certain TMF hydrographs), (4) number of repetitions of TMF cycles to 
minimize compensatory survival response, and (5) recruitment threshold of both rainbow and 
brown trout populations to trigger TMF implementation.

By Mariah Giardina,1 Josh Korman,2 Michael D. Yard,1 Scott Wright,1 Matt Kaplinski,1 and Glen Bennett 1
Introduction
In many waterways in the Western United States, particularly 
downstream from dams, rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) 
and brown trout (Salmo trutta) have been introduced to promote 
sport fishing. The introduction of nonnative species in certain 
instances have resulted in the development of abundant and 
self-sustaining populations, which can have negative effects on 
native fish assemblages through competition and predation (Yard 
and others, 2016; Yackulic and others, 2018; Healy and others, 
2020). Resource managers sometimes face the challenge of 
balancing mandates to promote sport fisheries and maintain or 
enhance endangered native fish populations (Dibble and others, 
2015). With a lack of evidence-based outcomes for invasive 
species control measures, many management actions fall short in 
effectively mitigating the negative effect of invasive species on 
native fish populations (Mueller, 2005).
Downstream from the Glen Canyon Dam in Arizona, the 
Colorado River is a highly regulated river system. The Glen 
Canyon Dam Adaptive Management Program, tasked with 
improving the condition of this ecosystem and other resources 
(water, hydropower, recreation, cultural, and others), has a 
mandate to protect federally threatened species in the Grand 
Canyon region of the Colorado River while simultaneously 
maintaining a nonnative rainbow trout sport fishery in Glen 
Canyon. Humpback chub (Gila cypha) are endemic to the 
Colorado River and the quality of their habitat has declined 
because of the construction and operation of the Glen Canyon 
Dam.

an increase in survival of early life history stages caused

2012; 2017).

Colorado River confluence if conditions in Lees Ferry were to

mechanical removal, (2) turbidity enhancement, and (3) TMFs. Of 
these actions, only mechanical removal has been evaluated using a 
large-scale field experiment (Coggins and others, 2011).

from 2003 to 2006 in lower Marble Canyon (control reach) and

removal reach also declined (Coggins and others, 2011). More

Little Colorado River reach is expected to overwhelm mechanical 
removal efforts (Bair and others, 2018). In addition, prescriptive 
measures using mechanical removal are costly and are not 
supported by local Native American Tribes. Mechanical removal 
is likely most effective during periods when trout immigration 
rates into the Little Colorado River reach are low, owing to 
lower population abundance combined with low abundance of 
humpback chub (Bair and others, 2018).
The goal of a turbidity enhancement strategy would be to 
increase turbidity levels in Marble Canyon to reduce growth rates 
of rainbow trout, either by adding fine-grained sediment into the 
system, or through management of fine-grained sediment that 
is naturally supplied by tributaries (Korman and others, 2021). 
This strategy was not considered as part of the LTEMP nor in 
the EIS analysis, though it was considered in early discussions of 
alternatives. Trout are visual sight feeders and low turbidity levels 
in late fall through early summer in Marble Canyon promote 
rainbow trout growth and successful reproduction.

title: A literature review and hypsometric analysis to support decisions on trout management flows on the Colorado River downstream from Glen Canyon Dam

chunk_text:
In addition, prescriptive 
measures using mechanical removal are costly and are not 
supported by local Native American Tribes. Mechanical removal 
is likely most effective during periods when trout immigration 
rates into the Little Colorado River reach are low, owing to 
lower population abundance combined with low abundance of 
humpback chub (Bair and others, 2018).
The goal of a turbidity enhancement strategy would be to 
increase turbidity levels in Marble Canyon to reduce growth rates 
of rainbow trout, either by adding fine-grained sediment into the 
system, or through management of fine-grained sediment that 
is naturally supplied by tributaries (Korman and others, 2021). 
This strategy was not considered as part of the LTEMP nor in 
the EIS analysis, though it was considered in early discussions of 
alternatives. Trout are visual sight feeders and low turbidity levels 
in late fall through early summer in Marble Canyon promote 
rainbow trout growth and successful reproduction. High turbidity 
can lead to substantial reductions in rainbow trout growth and 
conditions that can reduce spawning success and overall survival 
in Marble Canyon and downstream from the Little Colorado 
River (Korman and others, 2021). Consequently, flows that reduce 
turbidity may result in an increase in rainbow trout growth and 
reproduction in Marble Canyon, which can increase the number 
of rainbow trout near the Little Colorado River confluence. For 
example, autumn HFEs that are followed by high monthly flow 
volumes and hydropeaking during winter months may result 
in clearer water compared to an alternative without an HFE 
following sediment input from tributaries (Rubin and others, 
2002). HFEs resuspend sediment from the channel bed, deposit it 
on higher elevation sandbars, and export suspended fine-grained 
sediment from the system (Rubin and others, 2002). This process 
in turn reduces background turbidity levels, and therefore could 
help maintain high trout densities in Marble Canyon and the 
Little Colorado River. In years when trout density in Marble 
Literature Review 3
Canyon is high and there is sufficient sediment, leaving more 
fine-grained sediment on the bed could result in a longer period of 
elevated turbidity levels, which would help limit the abundance of 
rainbow trout near the Little Colorado River. Although the effects 
of turbidity on foraging and growth of rainbow trout are well 
established (Yard and others, 2011; Korman and others, 2021), 
there is still considerable uncertainty about the extent to which 
high winter flow volumes, winter hydropeaking, and autumn 
HFEs influence the turbidity regime in Marble Canyon, and how 
the effects of these processes vary with sediment supply.
Trout management flows are an experimental element 
identified in the LTEMP directed at limiting large recruitment 
events of rainbow trout (U.S. Department of Interior, 2016a, b, 
c). Owing to density-dependent factors, young rainbow trout 
produced in Glen Canyon disperse into Marble Canyon by 
midsummer (Korman and others, 2016). These young recruits can 
survive in Marble Canyon under suitable conditions, and slowly 
make their way down to the Little Colorado River (Korman and 
others, 2016, 2017; Yard and others, 2016).
Trout management flows are designed to reduce the survival 
of early life stages of rainbow trout in Glen Canyon to limit the 
extent of downstream dispersal into Marble Canyon. Because 
of the recent increase in brown trout in Glen Canyon (Runge 
and others, 2018; Yackulic and others, 2020), interest has been 
expressed in using TMFs to limit their abundance by substantially 
reducing or eliminating recruitment. However, since TMFs in the 
LTEMP were intendedfor rainbow trout, any application of this 
management strategy to brown trout would require regulatory 
changes to the LTEMP to account for the difference in time of 
year (earlier) required to target brown trout during their more 
vulnerable life history stages. Trout management flows designed 
for brown trout may also have to be altered if early life stage 
habitat use is centered more on deep, offshore habitats than 
shallow-edge habitats.
The purpose of this report is to address some of the critical 
uncertainties about rainbow trout and brown trout responses to 
TMFs. We provide: (1) a comprehensive literature review on fish 
stranding to identify the key factors affecting stranding, knowledge 
gaps, and possible research studies to reconcile uncertainties; 
(2) results of a hypsometric analysis that predicts stranding risk 
for age-0 trout in Glen Canyon under a range of TMFs using 
existing bathymetric data and flow and habitat suitability models; 
and lastly, (3) considerations on future research and monitoring 
for TMFs.
Literature Review
We conducted a literature review relevant to juvenile fish 
stranding in regulated rivers worldwide. Fish become stranded on 
the shoreline or in isolated pools when water levels drop quickly, 
often resulting in mortality. Fish stranding in regulated rivers can 
be caused by fluctuating flows due to hydropower operations but 
can also occur in unregulated rivers that have natural variation in 
flows (Thompson, 1970; Bauersfeld, 1978; Pflug and others, 1989; 
Hunter, 1992; Irvine and others, 2009; Nagrodski and others, 
2012). Most of the fish stranding literature is focused on mitigating 
stranding-related mortality resulting from hydropeaking flows on 
high-valued salmon and trout species. Only one study identified 
stranding as a strategy to control invasive fish populations, and it 
was conducted in a reservoir to promote the growth of smallmouth 
bass (Micropterus dolomieu) for recreational fishing by reducing 
the population of invasive bluegill (Lepomis macrochirus) (LeRoy 
Heman and others, 1969).
Consequently, the TMFs proposed in the LTEMP are a new 
management concept that has not been implemented or tested 
elsewhere. Reviewing the existing literature on fish stranding can 
help inform key elements of potential TMF hydrographs.
Methods
Data used in this study are provided in Korman and 
others (2024).
Literature Search
The literature review was based on results returned from 
two major search engines: Web of Science and Google Scholar. 
Multiple combinations of keywords were used in the search: 
strand*, entrap*, entrain*, fish kill, fish salvage, fish, juvenile fish, 
age 0 fish, salmonid, trout, hydropeak*, fish response to altered 
flow, flow regime, mortality, population effect, regulated river, 
hydropower, fluctuat*, dam effects, and dewater*. For searches in 
Google Scholar that generated more than 30,000 results, sources 
were sorted by “most relevant,” and the first 1,000 sources were 
evaluated for selection, or until there were multiple pages with 
no relevant results. In Web of Science, all search results were 
evaluated for selection. Using various combinations of keywords 
in both search engines resulted in over 40,000 sources. Following 
this, sources were selected based on two criteria: (1) included 
salmonid species (note: the few stranding papers focused on 
cyprinids were included to understand potential TMF impacts 
on humpback chub, but cyprinids were not specifically searched 
for in keywords as this was not primary focus of this paper), 
(2) the intent of the paper was to study stranding (whether 
observed, estimated, or modelled). These criteria eliminated 
papers on stranding of marine species and tropical fishes, as 
well as vessel-induced stranding. Similarly, other sources where 
fish stranding was due to anthropogenic structures that led to 
entrainment or entrapment were also excluded. A small percentage 
of relevant papers were reviews of the primary literature on 
stranding and associated variables; these secondary sources were 
excluded from the review to eliminate redundancy.
After applying the above selection criteria, 69 relevant 
papers were entered into a database (appendix 1). Each paper 
was evaluated for whether it addressed major factors influencing 
stranding, which include: (1) flow characteristics (flow range, 
duration of high and low flows, down-ramp rate, magnitude 
of stage change, frequency of flow fluctuations), (2) fish life 
stage and size class, (3) channel morphology (substrate, lateral 
4 Literature Review and Hypsometric Analysis on Trout Management Flows on the Colorado River
slope, and structural features), (4) diel cycle (night versus day), 
and (5) water temperature. The selected studies used varying 
metrics for the above factors or, in some cases, did not include 
specific factors. Therefore, we classified each study on whether 
it included each factor based on the following criteria: a factor 
was not included in study, a factor was identified in the study 
but not directly evaluated to quantify its effect, or a factor was 
evaluated (for example, a comparative analysis using a range of 
values) for effect on stranding.
Additionally, we searched the selected studies for the 
effect of stranding mortality events on long-term population 
trends to supplement our understanding of using stranding as a 
population-control mechanism.
Analysis of Flow, Light, and Stage for Glen Canyon
Since we evaluated flow characteristics and water 
temperature as factors influencing stranding in the literature 
review, we analyzed data on the physical characteristics of the 
Colorado River in Glen Canyon to provide site-specific context 
to interpret results from the literature review. Discharge and 
temperature data for the Colorado River were acquired from 
U.S. Geological Survey monitoring station at Lees Ferry (U.S. 
Geological Survey, 2022). Our analysis of the Glen Canyon Dam 
flow data is limited to only the winter, spring, and early summer 
(that is, January–July), is when stranding of young-of-year 
rainbow and brown trout would likely occur.

of the recent increase in brown trout in Glen Canyon (Runge 
and others, 2018; Yackulic and others, 2020), interest has been 
expressed in using TMFs to limit their abundance by substantially 
reducing or eliminating recruitment. However, since TMFs in the 
LTEMP were intendedfor rainbow trout, any application of this 
management strategy to brown trout would require regulatory 
changes to the LTEMP to account for the difference in time of 
year (earlier) required to target brown trout during their more 
vulnerable life history stages. Trout management flows designed 
for brown trout may also have to be altered if early life stage 
habitat use is centered more on deep, offshore habitats than 
shallow-edge habitats.
The purpose of this report is to address some of the critical 
uncertainties about rainbow trout and brown trout responses to 
TMFs. We provide: (1) a comprehensive literature review on fish 
stranding to identify the key factors affecting stranding, knowledge 
gaps, and possible research studies to reconcile uncertainties; 
(2) results of a hypsometric analysis that predicts stranding risk 
for age-0 trout in Glen Canyon under a range of TMFs using 
existing bathymetric data and flow and habitat suitability models; 
and lastly, (3) considerations on future research and monitoring 
for TMFs.
Literature Review
We conducted a literature review relevant to juvenile fish 
stranding in regulated rivers worldwide. Fish become stranded on 
the shoreline or in isolated pools when water levels drop quickly, 
often resulting in mortality. Fish stranding in regulated rivers can 
be caused by fluctuating flows due to hydropower operations but 
can also occur in unregulated rivers that have natural variation in 
flows (Thompson, 1970; Bauersfeld, 1978; Pflug and others, 1989; 
Hunter, 1992; Irvine and others, 2009; Nagrodski and others, 
2012). Most of the fish stranding literature is focused on mitigating 
stranding-related mortality resulting from hydropeaking flows on 
high-valued salmon and trout species. Only one study identified 
stranding as a strategy to control invasive fish populations, and it 
was conducted in a reservoir to promote the growth of smallmouth 
bass (Micropterus dolomieu) for recreational fishing by reducing 
the population of invasive bluegill (Lepomis macrochirus) (LeRoy 
Heman and others, 1969).
Consequently, the TMFs proposed in the LTEMP are a new 
management concept that has not been implemented or tested 
elsewhere. Reviewing the existing literature on fish stranding can 
help inform key elements of potential TMF hydrographs.
Methods
Data used in this study are provided in Korman and 
others (2024).
Literature Search
The literature review was based on results returned from 
two major search engines: Web of Science and Google Scholar. 
Multiple combinations of keywords were used in the search: 
strand*, entrap*, entrain*, fish kill, fish salvage, fish, juvenile fish, 
age 0 fish, salmonid, trout, hydropeak*, fish response to altered 
flow, flow regime, mortality, population effect, regulated river, 
hydropower, fluctuat*, dam effects, and dewater*. For searches in 
Google Scholar that generated more than 30,000 results, sources 
were sorted by “most relevant,” and the first 1,000 sources were 
evaluated for selection, or until there were multiple pages with 
no relevant results. In Web of Science, all search results were 
evaluated for selection. Using various combinations of keywords 
in both search engines resulted in over 40,000 sources. Following 
this, sources were selected based on two criteria: (1) included 
salmonid species (note: the few stranding papers focused on 
cyprinids were included to understand potential TMF impacts 
on humpback chub, but cyprinids were not specifically searched 
for in keywords as this was not primary focus of this paper), 
(2) the intent of the paper was to study stranding (whether 
observed, estimated, or modelled). These criteria eliminated 
papers on stranding of marine species and tropical fishes, as 
well as vessel-induced stranding. Similarly, other sources where 
fish stranding was due to anthropogenic structures that led to 
entrainment or entrapment were also excluded. A small percentage 
of relevant papers were reviews of the primary literature on 
stranding and associated variables; these secondary sources were 
excluded from the review to eliminate redundancy.
After applying the above selection criteria, 69 relevant 
papers were entered into a database (appendix 1). Each paper 
was evaluated for whether it addressed major factors influencing 
stranding, which include: (1) flow characteristics (flow range, 
duration of high and low flows, down-ramp rate, magnitude 
of stage change, frequency of flow fluctuations), (2) fish life 
stage and size class, (3) channel morphology (substrate, lateral 
4 Literature Review and Hypsometric Analysis on Trout Management Flows on the Colorado River
slope, and structural features), (4) diel cycle (night versus day), 
and (5) water temperature. The selected studies used varying 
metrics for the above factors or, in some cases, did not include 
specific factors. Therefore, we classified each study on whether 
it included each factor based on the following criteria: a factor 
was not included in study, a factor was identified in the study 
but not directly evaluated to quantify its effect, or a factor was 
evaluated (for example, a comparative analysis using a range of 
values) for effect on stranding.
Additionally, we searched the selected studies for the 
effect of stranding mortality events on long-term population 
trends to supplement our understanding of using stranding as a 
population-control mechanism.
Analysis of Flow, Light, and Stage for Glen Canyon
Since we evaluated flow characteristics and water 
temperature as factors influencing stranding in the literature 
review, we analyzed data on the physical characteristics of the 
Colorado River in Glen Canyon to provide site-specific context 
to interpret results from the literature review. Discharge and 
temperature data for the Colorado River were acquired from 
U.S. Geological Survey monitoring station at Lees Ferry (U.S. 
Geological Survey, 2022). Our analysis of the Glen Canyon Dam 
flow data is limited to only the winter, spring, and early summer 
(that is, January–July), is when stranding of young-of-year 
rainbow and brown trout would likely occur.

normal hydropeaking operations at Glen Canyon Dam, we 
separated daily discharges into two operational periods: pre-EIS 
and MLFF-LTEMP. We defined an early period between 1970 and 
1991 as pre-EIS but excluded flow records that were considered 
anomalous because of operational changes from filling regimes 
(March 15–June 30, 1977), tests (June 1–30, 1980), or flood 
risk (1983–87). We defined a later Modified Low Fluctuating 
Flow (MLFF) period between 1992 and 2016, but we excluded 
experimental flows (March 23–April 7, 1996; March 26–June 30, 
2000; March 5, 2008), high flows (1997–98), and reservoir 
equalization operations (2011). Since the current operations under 
the LTEMP have not significantly changed from the MLFF period 
(except for monthly water distribution and the down-ramp rate, 
which we address where necessary), we grouped these operations 
between 1992 and 2022 as MLFF-LTEMP for the purposes of 
this paper. We calculated several flow characteristics for the two 
periods, including (1) the average monthly minimum flow, (2) the 
average monthly down-ramp rate based on highest hourly rate 
encountered per day, (3) the mean monthly standard deviation of 
daily flow minimums and mean monthly standard deviation of 
daily down-ramp rates, and (4) the daily flow range (maximum 
minus minimum).
To compare the effects of flow variation reported in the 
literature with those in the Colorado River, we calculated 
the stage change in Glen Canyon using stage-discharge 
relationships (Randle and Pemberton, 1987). Exposure of the 
river bottom to direct sunlight following decreases in stage 
height will expose stranded fish to warmer water temperatures, 
which will have a negative impact on their survival. We 
therefore calculated the average time of day when direct 
sunlight strikes the mid-channel of Glen Canyon using a solar 
model that accounts for topographic obstruction and solar 
declination (Yard and others, 2005). Estimates of solar exposure 
are based on mid-river points at 100-meter intervals from 
Lees Ferry upstream to Glen Canyon Dam. For comparison, 
we calculated solar exposure on two different dates that 
would reflect conditions during TMFs targeting brown trout 
(March 21) and rainbow trout (June 1). These dates reflect a 
period of peak emergence based on average water temperatures.
Findings
General Overview of Stranding Literature
Of the 69 stranding papers analyzed, 59 percent were 
peer-reviewed journal articles, 33 percent were technical reports (9 
of the 23 technical reports were conducted on the Hanford Reach 
of the Columbia River), 4 percent were conference papers, and 3 
percent were graduate or doctoral theses. More than 73 percent 
of the studies were published in the last 20 years. Rainbow trout 
and (or) brown trout were included in 52 percent (36) of the 69 
stranding studies. Table 1 provides an overview of the extent that 
the stranding literature quantifies factors influencing stranding. 
Structural complexity (37 studies) and down-ramp rate (26 
studies) were the factors most evaluated for effect on stranding. 
Although life stage was the most common factor identified in 
the 69 stranding papers, it was only quantified for its effect on 
stranding outcome in 17 studies.
In reviewing the existing stranding literature, we found 
that the major factors contributing to stranding are highly 
interdependent and site-specific. For example, the effects of 
ramping rates will depend on channel morphology. Effects of flow 
regime on stranding can vary substantially between winter and 
summer, and between night and day.

Most of the reviewed literature evaluated fluctuating flow 
characteristics and the effects on fish stranding. In total, 86 
percent of the studies were conducted on regulated rivers. In

power generation, which resulted in considerable variation of 
flows within a day. In studies of smaller volume rivers, some 
dams served as water storage facilities and were subject to 
more constant releases within a day, and instead flows varied 
only by season to meet downstream water needs. As such, 
the metrics used to quantify each flow-related factor varied 
across studies, making comparisons difficult. Some of the 
metrics included the flow range (minimum and maximum), 
duration of time under high and low flows (that is, shoreline 
habitat inundation or “wetted history”), down-ramp rate, stage 
change, and frequency of flow fluctuations, as defined below. 
We used data from Glen Canyon Dam to put literature review 
results into context (U.S. Geological Survey, 2022).
Literature Review 5
Flow Range
Flow range is the difference between maximum and 
minimum flows over a specific time interval. Higher flow

period, primarily due to differences in mean flows between
